title: Number Sense & Estimation
coreInsight: Numbers carry magnitude and structure; estimation and reasonableness can reveal what an exact answer should look like before calculation.
narrativeTransition: Start with calculations that can be done exactly but become much easier once the learner estimates, decomposes, or compares magnitude first.
commonMisconceptions: Exact calculation is always better than estimation.
An answer that comes from valid arithmetic does not need a reasonableness check.
The written form of a number is more important than its magnitude or structure.

title: Fractions, Decimals & Percents
coreInsight: Fractions, decimals, and percents are different representations of the same quantities, and a fraction is itself a number with a location and magnitude.
narrativeTransition: Whole numbers leave gaps on the number line. Build and compare quantities inside those gaps, then show that fraction, decimal, and percent notation can name the same point.
commonMisconceptions: The numerator and denominator behave like two independent whole numbers.
A larger denominator automatically means a larger fraction.
More decimal digits automatically means a larger number.
A percent has meaning without identifying the whole it is a percent of.

title: Ratios & Proportions
coreInsight: A ratio describes a multiplicative relationship or repeatable batch, and proportional situations preserve that relationship as quantities scale.
narrativeTransition: Fractions compare a part with a whole; now compare two quantities directly and ask what must stay the same when both quantities scale.
commonMisconceptions: Ratio problems should be solved by additive differences.
Part-to-part and part-to-whole ratios are interchangeable.
Cross-multiplication is the meaning of proportion rather than one consequence of it.
Corresponding quantities can be paired in any order.

title: Rates, Units & Proportional Reasoning
coreInsight: A rate is a ratio connecting quantities with different units, and the units themselves reveal how the quantities relate.
narrativeTransition: Attach units to the two sides of a ratio—miles per hour, dollars per item, pages per minute—and let the unit language expose the operation.
commonMisconceptions: Units can be ignored once numbers are written down.
Rate and total amount are the same kind of quantity.
Every rate problem is direct proportion.
The word per can be treated as decoration rather than division.

title: Percent Change
coreInsight: Percent change measures change relative to a specific base, and that base can change from one step to the next.
narrativeTransition: Use the proportional meaning of percent to describe a change, then make a second change so the learner sees that the reference whole has moved.
commonMisconceptions: Successive percent changes simply add.
Reverse percentage problems can use the final amount as the original base.
Percentage points and percent change are the same thing.
A 20% increase followed by a 20% decrease returns to the start.

title: Averages & Basic Statistics
coreInsight: The mean is the equal-share or balance value determined by a total, while median, mode, and range describe different features of a data set.
narrativeTransition: Redistribute unequal piles until all piles are equal, then connect the balanced height to total divided by count.
commonMisconceptions: The mean must be one of the observed data values.
Average always means the middle value.
Averages of groups can be averaged without considering group sizes.
The mean can be manipulated without tracking the underlying total.

title: Graphs, Tables & Data
coreInsight: Graphs and tables encode relationships; scale, position, shape, and change all carry mathematical meaning.
narrativeTransition: After summarizing data numerically, represent the same information visually and ask what becomes visible that was hard to see in a list.
commonMisconceptions: A graph is a picture of a real scene rather than a representation of variables.
Axis scale can be ignored.
A taller point or bar always means a faster rate of change.
Reading one value is the same as understanding the trend.
